channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: A magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia, killing more than 100 people and closing six airports, while China earmarked CNY 380 million in relief after Typhoon Dolphin battered its eastern industrial provinces.
item.description:
Natural disasters hit two regions hard. A magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on the morning of 10 August, with its epicentre near San José del Palmar in Chocó province, killing more than 100 people and causing heavy damage across a cluster of cities in the Andean foothills; buildings cracked in the provincial capital Quibdó, rescuers searched rubble in Cali, and six airports in the west (Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura) suspended operations, though the largest cities Bogotá and Medellín were largely spared. On the other side of the world, China's finance and emergency-management ministries earmarked CNY 180 million from the central disaster-relief fund — CNY 120 million for five eastern provinces (Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Anhui, Fujian and Jiangxi) hit by Typhoon Dolphin and flooding, the rest for drought in Inner Mongolia and Xinjiang — while the planning agency added CNY 200 million to rebuild roads, water works, hospitals and schools in Zhejiang.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers the immediate relevance is supply-chain and demand disruption in affected industrial and logistics zones, followed by reconstruction demand. China's eastern provinces are dense manufacturing and chemical-production hubs, so typhoon damage and the relief effort point to short-term disruption and then a rebuild that consumes construction chemicals, sealants and coatings. Colombia's quake is primarily a humanitarian and regional-logistics event, but reconstruction of damaged buildings and infrastructure will lift demand for building materials and repair chemistries in the medium term. The broader theme, consistent across recent alerts, is that natural disasters are a recurring operating variable requiring resilient logistics and contingency planning.

The New York Times | Lianhe Zaobao | Xinhua

item.title: German new-car registrations edged up 1.2% in July, driven by a 61.7% surge in battery-electric cars to a 29.3% market share, even as German commercial-property prices slipped 1% — a mixed read on Europe's largest economy.
item.description:
Germany's demand signals were mixed but tilted positive on autos. The Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) reported 268,068 new passenger-car registrations in July 2026, up 1.2% year-on-year, with the story firmly electric: battery-electric registrations jumped 61.7% to 78,609 vehicles, a 29.3% share of the market, while petrol and diesel registrations fell 29.7% and 21.8% respectively, and average new-car CO2 dropped 15.1% to 91.2 grams per kilometre. State purchase subsidies continue to drive the electric surge. On the property side, though, Germany's fragile recovery stalled: the VDP banking association reported commercial real-estate prices (offices and retail) fell 1% year-on-year in the second quarter after a 0.5% gain in the first, while residential prices still rose 1.9%. VDP's chief executive said commercial property is reacting more sharply than housing to geopolitics, rising inflation expectations and interest rates.

Industry Impact

Both readings map onto ACS end-markets. The electric-vehicle surge is structurally positive for suppliers positioned in e-mobility chemistry — battery-pack bonding and sealing, thermal management and structural adhesives, which are used more intensively in electric than in combustion cars — partly offsetting the long German auto slump flagged in recent alerts. The dip in commercial property, by contrast, is a caution for construction-linked coatings, sealants and adhesives tied to offices and retail, where demand is most rate- and confidence-sensitive. The combined signal supports reweighting toward automotive e-mobility applications and staying cautious on German commercial-construction volumes.

Yahoo Germany | MarketScreener

item.title: Nvidia is in talks with Wall Street heavyweights on a USD 500 billion AI-infrastructure funding package, while TSMC and Sony agreed to invest about USD 6.3 billion in a Japanese joint venture to mass-produce next-generation image sensors from 2029.
item.description:
The build-out of AI and advanced electronics is drawing enormous capital. According to the Financial Times, chipmaker Nvidia is partnering with a group of US investment giants — Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR — on a USD 500 billion funding package for AI-infrastructure projects such as data centres, though details of the structure and how much is new money were not disclosed. In parallel, Taiwan's TSMC and Japan's Sony are forming a joint venture — roughly 40% TSMC, 60% Sony — to develop and manufacture next-generation image sensors for smartphones, cars and robots at Sony's Kumamoto site in Japan, investing about JPY 1 trillion (USD 6.3 billion) with mass production targeted for 2029 and output reportedly bound for Apple iPhones. Both deals underline how semiconductors, sensors and data-centre capacity are now among the largest destinations for global industrial investment.

Industry Impact

Electronics and semiconductors are a fast-growing, materials-intensive frontier for ACS. Data-centre and AI-hardware build-outs consume thermal-interface materials, encapsulants, conformal coatings and structural adhesives, while advanced image-sensor and chip manufacturing relies on specialty bonding, underfill and protective chemistries. A USD 500 billion AI-infrastructure programme and a multi-billion-dollar sensor fab both point to durable demand growth in these high-value segments — and reward suppliers that can qualify into demanding electronics and semiconductor processes. For ACS producers the opportunity is to attach to the AI and sensor supply chains; the risk is that this capacity concentrates in the US and East Asia, away from a stagnating Europe.

South China Morning Post | Handelsblatt | Euronews | Cnyes | Commercial Times | Chinatimes

item.title: Global drugmakers including Pfizer, Eli Lilly and AstraZeneca have pledged roughly USD 500 billion in US investment to dodge threatened pharma tariffs, as officials scramble to close the supply-chain gaps a tariff-driven reshoring surge has exposed.
item.description:
US industrial policy is pulling major manufacturing investment onshore. Pharmaceutical companies including Eli Lilly, Pfizer, AstraZeneca and Roche have announced roughly USD 500 billion of US investment to strengthen infrastructure, reduce supply-chain risk and reassure investors amid the threat of sector-specific "pharma tariffs." Pfizer struck a deal with President Trump in late September to invest USD 70 billion in US research and manufacturing in return for a three-year exemption from those tariffs, and Britain's GSK plans USD 30 billion over five years. The reshoring wave is broader than pharma: Treasury and Small Business Administration officials told Reuters that Trump's import tariffs and deregulation are fuelling a surge in foreign direct investment into US manufacturing, but said they are now working with investors to identify gaps in domestic supply chains and help small and mid-sized firms scale up to supply the new plants — an admission that components and inputs are not yet available to match the announced capacity.

Industry Impact

Large-scale US reshoring is a double-edged development for ACS producers. A wave of new pharmaceutical and manufacturing plants expands demand for high-specification adhesives, coatings, sealants and process chemistries — pharma and medical applications are premium, regulation-heavy segments where qualified suppliers command higher margins. At the same time, the officials' warning about supply-chain gaps signals localisation pressure: customers building in the US will increasingly want their input suppliers, including chemical and ACS producers, to serve them locally rather than import. The strategic implication is to align US capacity and technical support with the reshoring pipeline, particularly in high-value medical, electronics and industrial applications.

BNN Bloomberg | MarketScreener

item.title: Singapore more than doubled the floor of its 2026 growth forecast to 4.5–5.5% on the global AI investment boom, after second-quarter GDP rose 5.9%, while Vietnam's manufacturing PMI climbed to 52.9 — signs of resilient Southeast Asian demand.
item.description:
Southeast Asia is emerging as a relative bright spot. Singapore's Ministry of Trade and Industry raised its 2026 growth forecast on 11 August from 2.0–4.0% to 4.5–5.5%, citing a stronger-than-expected global artificial-intelligence investment boom and a milder-than-feared hit from the Middle East war in the second half. The upgrade followed second-quarter GDP growth of 5.9% year-on-year (above the 5.7% advance estimate), taking first-half growth to 6.1%. Vietnam added to the positive picture: its S&P Global manufacturing PMI — where a reading above 50 signals expansion — rose to 52.9 in July from 51.8, its strongest since February, and seven export categories each topped USD 10 billion in the first seven months, led by electronics, computers and components at over USD 85 billion. The readings suggest that AI-driven capital spending and continued supply-chain relocation into the region are outweighing the war-driven drag felt elsewhere.

Industry Impact

ASEAN is a priority growth region for ACS demand, tied to the electronics, packaging, automotive and construction manufacturing that keeps relocating into the bloc. Singapore's rare upward revision and Vietnam's expanding factory sector confirm the region as a destination for new production capacity that will need industrial adhesives, coatings and sealants, with the AI-hardware and electronics build-out especially material for high-value bonding and encapsulation chemistries. The signal for suppliers is to keep tilting capacity and commercial focus toward the strongest ASEAN economies, which are decoupling from the European and Chinese slowdowns.

MarketScreener | CNA | VietnamPlus

item.title: Morgan Stanley cut its 2026 forecasts for China's property market — new-construction starts down 20% — as land sales slump, even as Beijing accelerates a nationwide urban-renewal programme to support construction demand.
item.description:
China's property downturn is proving stubborn. Morgan Stanley lowered its 2026 forecasts for the sector, cutting expected new-construction starts by 20%, real-estate investment by 17% and new-home sales by 9.8%, blaming weak land sales: the transaction area of land across 300 cities tracked by the China Index Academy fell 21% year-on-year in the first seven months, which had already dragged first-half construction starts down 23%. The bank kept China Resources Land as its top pick, suggesting selective resilience among the strongest developers. Offsetting the new-build weakness, Beijing is leaning on renovation: its "15th Five-Year Plan" for urban renewal is accelerating projects nationwide — renovating ageing residential blocks, upgrading underground pipe networks and revitalising historic districts — with Wuhan the first megacity to launch a formal plan, kicking off what officials frame as a systematic upgrade of existing urban space.

Industry Impact

Construction is one of the largest end-markets for ACS products — tile adhesives, sealants, waterproofing and architectural coatings — so a further 20% cut to Chinese housing starts is a clear negative for new-build-linked demand. But the pivot to urban renewal partly cushions the blow: renovation and infrastructure upgrades consume repair mortars, sealants, waterproofing and coatings, often at higher value per project than volume new-build. For suppliers the implication is to reweight toward China's renovation, retrofit and infrastructure segments rather than greenfield residential construction, and to track which developers and city-renewal programmes actually get funded as the demand base shifts.

Commercial Times | Caijing

item.title: China's investment in advanced manufacturing jumped 73.1% year-on-year in July, with AI-related patent grants up 60%, underlining Beijing's push to build out high-tech industry even as consumer spending grew only modestly.
item.description:
China is pouring money into the industries it wants to lead. The National Development and Reform Commission's information centre reported that capital investment in advanced manufacturing rose 73.1% year-on-year in July 2026, a striking acceleration that signals continued state-backed expansion of high-tech production capacity. Patent grants tied to "strategic emerging industries" rose 10.7%, and artificial-intelligence-related patent grants jumped 60%. The consumer side was far more subdued: total consumption payments rose just 2.2% year-on-year on big-data measures, with goods up about 4% but services up only 0.4%; a bright spot was an 8.5% rise in spending on household appliances and audiovisual equipment, up nearly 11 points on the previous month, likely helped by trade-in subsidies. The pattern fits Beijing's strategy of driving growth through investment in advanced manufacturing and "new productive forces" while consumer demand recovers only slowly — and it dovetails with the stimulus signals policymakers have been flagging.

Industry Impact

A 73% surge in advanced-manufacturing investment is a strong demand signal for the specialty adhesives, coatings and sealants used in electronics, batteries, robotics, electric vehicles and high-tech assembly — the segments China is prioritising. It also means faster build-out of domestic Chinese suppliers of the very materials Western chemical firms sell, deepening both the opportunity and the competitive threat. For ACS producers the read is to align with the high-growth Chinese segments (electronics and new-energy chemistry) while recognising that subsidised local capacity will keep pricing pressure high. The soft consumer numbers, meanwhile, temper hopes for a broad packaging- and consumer-goods-led demand rebound.

China Economic Net

item.title: Washington is set to hit more than 500 categories of Canadian goods with 50% tariffs from 19 August, and the damage from US auto tariffs is already showing next door, with Mexican light-vehicle exports down 9.7% in July.
item.description:
US tariff pressure on its two North American neighbours intensified. President Trump is threatening new 50% tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods from 19 August — more than 500 product categories, spanning items tied to specific irritants (provincial boycotts of US alcohol, Canada's protected dairy system) and, in Ottawa's telling, a grab-bag of seemingly unrelated products — in a fresh escalation of the trade war. Further south, the effect of existing US auto tariffs is already measurable: Mexican light-vehicle exports fell 9.7% year-on-year in July and production dropped 2.2%, according to statistics agency INEGI, with a Mexican commentator headlining the trend "the auto tariff is already biting Mexico." Over January–July, Mexican vehicle exports and production are down 0.3% and 0.7% respectively — modest so far, but deteriorating sharply in the latest month as the tariffs feed through.

Industry Impact

North America's tightly integrated automotive and construction supply chains are core ACS end-markets, so both developments bear directly on demand. A 50% blanket tariff on Canadian goods would raise the landed cost of building materials, metals and components on both sides of the border and disrupt cross-border chemical, paper and packaging flows; the Mexican export slump shows how auto tariffs translate into lower vehicle output — and therefore less demand for the structural adhesives, sealants and coatings that go into cars. Suppliers with cross-border operations should plan for customs complexity, retaliation risk and softer automotive volumes, while watching for last-minute deals that could reverse the tariffs as abruptly as they arrive.

The Globe and Mail | El Financiero

item.title: Ahead of an expected September Xi–Trump summit, Washington let Hong Kong sanctions on nine officials lapse, even as Beijing hit US and Mexican pecans with anti-dumping duties up to 54% and the US drafted a ban on Chinese data-centre components.
item.description:
The US–China relationship showed both thaw and friction in the run-up to a planned September summit between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. On the conciliatory side, Washington's decision not to renew its Hong Kong-related state of emergency effectively lifted sanctions on nine mainland Chinese and Hong Kong officials, which Beijing's Commerce Ministry welcomed as a step toward stabilising ties after Trump's May visit to China. On the combative side, China's Commerce Ministry issued a preliminary ruling that US and Mexican pecans had been "dumped," imposing anti-dumping deposits of 54.3% on US nuts (no US firm took part in the probe) and 17.8%–51.6% on Mexican ones from 11 August — a pointed pre-summit signal. Meanwhile the US Federal Communications Commission, now a spearhead of Trump's China-tech policy, is drafting a ban on imports of new Chinese data-centre components, having already blocked new Chinese drones, routers, inverters and robots and moved to bar Chinese labs from certifying electronics for the US market; China has answered with its own drone-and-tech export curbs.

Industry Impact

The mixed signals matter to ACS producers because the summit's outcome will set the tone for the tariff-and-tech environment that shapes chemical trade, electronics-linked demand and China operations. Sanctions relief hints at a possible de-escalation that would steady cross-border investment; the pecan duties and the FCC hardware ban show how quickly either side still reaches for trade weapons, and how the electronics and data-centre supply chains — a growth end-market for adhesives and coatings — are being redrawn along security lines. The read-through is to keep China-exposure scenarios live in both directions and to watch the summit as a genuine inflection point.

South China Morning Post | People's Daily | Bloomberg | The Standard | MarketScreener

item.title: Heat and drought could cost the EU around €180 billion this year — roughly 1% of GDP — with a study putting Italy's exposure at €74 billion, as France braces for its worst drought in 40 years and prepares billions in farm aid.
item.description:
The summer's heat and drought are turning into a measurable macro shock for Europe. Dutch lender Triodos Bank estimates losses of around €180 billion in 2026 — close to 1% of EU GDP — as agriculture, energy, transport and labour all come under strain; since the European Commission expects only 1.1% EU growth this year, realised losses on that scale could erase much of it. A study by Italy's CMCC climate foundation and the Politecnico di Milano warns a prolonged drought under 2°C of warming could cost Italy €74 billion and 960,000 jobs, while pointing to water recycling as a partial remedy. Austria's crop insurer already tallies €1 billion in agricultural damage. France is the acute case: the farm union FNSEA says growers need "several billion euros" after the worst drought in 40 years, with corn heading for its lowest harvest in four decades and some silage-corn losses of 90–100%; Agriculture Minister Genevard is preparing a national "Heatwave–Drought–Fires" support plan, and local emergency aid has already begun.

Industry Impact

The drought hits ACS demand indirectly but broadly. A blow of up to 1% of EU GDP saps the construction and manufacturing activity that drives adhesives, coatings and sealants across Henkel's largest region, and the fiscal cost of farm bailouts crowds out other spending. Water stress also raises the cost of bio-based and agricultural feedstocks and reinforces the river-logistics problems flagged in the chemical-squeeze story (see other insight in this alert). One constructive angle: the Italian study's emphasis on water recycling points to growing demand for water-treatment and efficiency chemistries. Overall it strengthens the case for building climate disruption into European demand and cost planning as a recurring, not exceptional, factor.

Dünya Gazetesi | The Economic Times | Il Sole 24 Ore | Reussir | Le Figaro | Der Standard

item.title: The EU imposed new anti-dumping duties of up to 24.1% on terephthalic acid — the raw material for PET plastic — from South Korea and Mexico, as Germany advanced a Circular Economy Act amendment set to tighten recycled-content and substance rules.
item.description:
Brussels tightened its grip on the chemical value chain on two fronts. The European Commission imposed anti-dumping duties — extra import taxes meant to offset goods sold below fair value — on terephthalic acid (PTA), the feedstock used to make PET plastic, at 6.1%–13.3% for South Korean material and 24.1% for Mexican material, to shield producers in Spain, Poland and Belgium. Separately, Germany is amending its Circular Economy Act (KrWG) to transpose the EU's revised Waste Framework Directive; the steel-industry association welcomed the draft's stronger emphasis on "raw-material sovereignty" but pressed for recycling, by-products and internal loops to count as strategic raw-material sources, for waste, product and chemicals law to be handled together so substance restrictions don't block functioning recycling, and for public procurement to mandate recycled content. It also warned that definitions for material versus chemical recycling should be set uniformly at EU — not national — level to avoid new bureaucracy and legal uncertainty.

Industry Impact

Both moves land squarely in Henkel's ACS markets. PTA duties raise the cost and reshuffle the sourcing of PET and polyester chemistry that sits close to packaging and coatings supply chains, and signal the EU's readiness to use trade defence inside the chemical feedstock chain — a pattern that can spread to other intermediates. The Circular Economy Act is more strategic still: rules on recyclability, recycled-content mandates and how chemicals law interacts with recycling directly shape demand for recyclable-compatible adhesives and coatings and for compliant, PFAS-free formulations (a theme running through recent alerts). Firms with recycled-content-ready, design-for-recycling chemistries stand to gain as procurement rules harden; those slow to adapt face both duty exposure and compliance risk.

MarketScreener | Wirtschaftsvereinigung Stahl | Wirtschaftsvereinigung Stahl

item.title: Low water on the Rhine is again threatening German chemical plants just as a Hormuz-driven oil shortage leaves parts of China's chemical industry short of feedstock, while Hungary's chemical sector cut nearly 200 MW of energy use to steady the grid.
item.description:
Europe's chemical heartland is being squeezed from two directions at once. Germany's Rhine — the artery its chemical industry relies on for cooling water, steam and cheap bulk transport of raw materials and finished chemicals — has fallen so low that riverside plants face rising costs and possible constraints, with far more cargo than usual pushed onto trucks and rail. The German retail association HDE is urging Berlin to permanently allow "long trucks" (oversized units that can each replace up to 1.5 conventional trucks and cut CO2 by up to 25%) to relieve the bottleneck. The strain is not only European: because oil tankers cannot clear the Strait of Hormuz, parts of China's chemical industry are, as one report put it, "on life support" — short of imported feedstock while higher oil prices lift their own export costs. Energy stress is spreading too: Hungary's chemical industry cut energy and water use by nearly 200 MW — about a quarter of the country's total savings — at the government's request to support grid stability, with big producers such as BorsodChem, MOL Petrolkémia and Nitrogénművek taking part.

Industry Impact

This is Henkel's core operating environment. Low Rhine levels raise inbound feedstock and outbound shipping costs across the German chemical corridor and can force allocation or output curbs at riverside sites; the long-truck workaround helps only at the margin and adds road-freight cost. The simultaneous Asian feedstock crunch shows the Hormuz disruption is now tightening raw-material supply globally, not just lifting prices, so shortages in one region ripple into pricing everywhere. Hungary's forced curtailment is a reminder that energy-intensive chemical production remains hostage to Europe's fragile power and water systems. The practical response: pre-position inventory, qualify non-river logistics, and keep energy hedges through the dry season.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | MAVESZ

item.title: Oil rebounded about 3% after Iran hardened its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and the IMF's latest figures show the war pushing Gulf economies into contraction, with Saudi output down 4.8% in the second quarter.
item.description:
Oil prices rose about 3% on 10 August after Iran said the United States must lift sanctions, pay reparations and meet further conditions before the Strait of Hormuz — the channel that carried a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war began in late February — can reopen. The move reversed a 7%-plus slide last week, when hopes ran high that Iran and Oman were close to a deal on new shipping lanes. Tehran says it is nearing a final pact with Oman but insists Washington first lift its naval blockade, withdraw forces, remove all sanctions and unfreeze Iranian assets. President Trump called the negotiations "half-hearted"; Vice-President Vance said the US would "verify, not trust" and that Iran had not yet delivered everything Washington wants. The economic toll is now visible in hard data: the IMF, which has cut its 2026 global growth forecast to 3% (its second cut this year), reports Saudi GDP fell 4.8% year-on-year in the second quarter — its first drop in three years, with the oil sector down 24.7% — and projects 2026 contractions of 8.6% in Qatar, 6.8% in Iraq and 6.1% in Iran.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry, the war remains the single biggest swing factor for input costs. A closed Hormuz keeps oil, naphtha, solvent and freight prices elevated and volatile, and the on-again/off-again diplomacy means sharp price moves in both directions on headlines rather than fundamentals. The IMF's Gulf contraction figures confirm the conflict is now denting real demand, not just prices — a drag on Middle Eastern construction and industrial activity. Producers should keep energy hedges and feedstock buffer stocks in place and treat any single-day oil swing as noise until a Hormuz reopening is actually confirmed.

Business Recorder | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Asharq Al-Awsat | China Economic Net | Challenges
